# Use case 3: microbial co-occurrence networks

Here, we will use __GraphExperiment__ to store microbial association networks
inferred from 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing data, with taxon-taxon networks
in `rowGraphs` and a sample-sample network in `colGraphs`. We will use the
`peerj13075` data set from the __mia__ package, a core package of the
miaverse ecosystem [@borman2025orchestrating], which
contains skin microbiota profiles of 58 genetically unrelated
Indian individuals from three different cities and with different diets
(vegetarian and mixed) [@potbhare2022skin].

Microbiome abundance data are *compositional*, i.e., sequencing only
provides information on the relative abundances of taxa. Thus, standard
correlation measures (e.g., Pearson's or Spearman's correlations) can lead to
spurious associations [@friedman2012inferring; @gloor2017microbiome].
To account for compositionality, we will use two widely used methods
implemented in the __SpiecEasi__ package: SPIEC-EASI [@kurtz2015sparse],
which infers a sparse graphical model (i.e., conditional dependencies
between taxa) from centered log-ratio (CLR)-transformed data, and SparCC
[@friedman2012inferring], which estimates correlations
between the underlying (log-transformed) absolute abundances.

```{r here}
#| message: false
#| eval: true

library(here)
library(GraphExperiment)
library(mia)
library(scater)
library(SpiecEasi)
library(bluster)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggraph)
library(patchwork)

set.seed(123) # for reproducibility
```

## Data description and processing

The data are stored in a `TreeSummarizedExperiment` object, the core data
structure of the miaverse ecosystem [@huang2021treesummarizedexperiment].
Taxa were already agglomerated at the genus level.

```{r}
# Load data
data("peerj13075", package = "mia")
tse <- peerj13075
tse

# Sample metadata
table(tse$Geographical_location, tse$Diet)
```

Since rare taxa provide little information for network inference, we will
only keep genera with at least one read in at least 20% of the samples.
Then, we will add a CLR-transformed assay, which we will use later.

```{r}
# Keep only prevalent genera
tse <- subsetByPrevalent(tse, detection = 1, prevalence = 0.2)
dim(tse)

# Add CLR-transformed assay
tse <- transformAssay(tse, method = "clr", pseudocount = 1)
```

Like `GraphExperiment`, `TreeSummarizedExperiment` extends the
`SingleCellExperiment` class. Hence, we can easily coerce a
`TreeSummarizedExperiment` object to a `GraphExperiment` object.
Tree-specific slots (`rowTree`, `colTree`, etc.) are not kept,
but they could be stored in the `metadata` slot if needed (see
use cases 6 and 7 for examples on how to handle phylogenies).

```{r}
# Coerce `TreeSummarizedExperiment` to `GraphExperiment`
ge <- as(tse, "GraphExperiment")
ge
```

## Inferring taxon-taxon association networks

Now, we will infer an association network with SPIEC-EASI using the
Meinshausen-Bühlmann neighborhood selection method, with the
sparsity parameter selected with the StARS approach
[@liu2010stability]. Note that `spiec.easi()` expects samples in rows
and taxa in columns, and it performs CLR transformation internally.

```{r}
# Infer network with SPIEC-EASI
counts <- t(assay(ge, "counts"))
se_mb <- spiec.easi(
    counts, method = "mb", lambda.min.ratio = 1e-3, nlambda = 30,
    pulsar.params = list(rep.num = 50, seed = 123)
)

# Get edge weights (symmetrized regression coefficients)
mb_weights <- as.matrix(symBeta(getOptBeta(se_mb), mode = "maxabs"))
dimnames(mb_weights) <- list(colnames(counts), colnames(counts))

# Create igraph object
g_spieceasi <- graph_from_adjacency_matrix(
    mb_weights, mode = "undirected", weighted = TRUE, diag = FALSE
)
E(g_spieceasi)$sign <- ifelse(E(g_spieceasi)$weight > 0, "positive", "negative")

g_spieceasi
```

Next, we will estimate SparCC correlations, and use 100 bootstrap
replicates to obtain P-values. We will keep only edges with
P < 0.05 and absolute correlations $\geq$ 0.3.

```{r}
# Estimate SparCC correlations with bootstrap P-values
sparcc_boot <- sparccboot(counts, R = 100)
sparcc_p <- pval.sparccboot(sparcc_boot)

# Create matrices of correlations and P-values
n <- ncol(counts)
sparcc_cor <- sparcc_pval <- matrix(
    0, n, n, dimnames = list(colnames(counts), colnames(counts))
)
sparcc_cor[upper.tri(sparcc_cor)] <- sparcc_p$cors
sparcc_pval[upper.tri(sparcc_pval)] <- sparcc_p$pvals

# Keep only significant correlations
sparcc_cor[sparcc_pval >= 0.05 | abs(sparcc_cor) < 0.3] <- 0

# Create igraph object
g_sparcc <- graph_from_adjacency_matrix(
    sparcc_cor, mode = "upper", weighted = TRUE, diag = FALSE
)
E(g_sparcc)$sign <- ifelse(E(g_sparcc)$weight > 0, "positive", "negative")

g_sparcc
```

Both networks were inferred from the same features, so they can be stored
together in the `rowGraphs` slot. We will also add node degrees
as node attributes.

```{r}
# Add node degree as node attributes
V(g_spieceasi)$degree <- degree(g_spieceasi)
V(g_sparcc)$degree <- degree(g_sparcc)

# Add graphs to `rowGraphs`
rowGraphs(ge) <- list(spieceasi = g_spieceasi, sparcc = g_sparcc)

ge
```

## Inferring a sample-sample network

Microbiome data are often explored at the sample level, e.g., to
identify groups of samples with similar community compositions. Here, we
will create a k-nearest neighbor (kNN) graph of samples based on
Aitchison distances (i.e., Euclidean distances of CLR-transformed data)
with __bluster__ [@lun2025bluster]. For that, we will first perform a
principal component analysis on the CLR-transformed data with
__scater__ [@mccarthy2017scater], and then build the kNN graph from
the top 10 principal components. Then, we will identify communities in
this graph with the Louvain algorithm, and store community assignments
as node attributes.

```{r}
# Perform PCA on CLR-transformed data
ge <- runPCA(ge, assay.type = "clr", ncomponents = 10)

# Build kNN graph of samples
g_samples <- makeKNNGraph(reducedDim(ge, "PCA"), k = 5)
V(g_samples)$name <- colnames(ge)

# Identify communities of samples
V(g_samples)$community <- as.character(membership(cluster_louvain(g_samples)))

# Add graph to `colGraphs`
colGraph(ge, "aitchison_knn") <- g_samples

ge
```

Note that the `GraphExperiment` object now contains assays, taxon and
sample metadata, principal components, and graphs of both
taxa and samples. As node attributes are added to
`rowData` and `colData`, we can explore how communities of samples
are associated with sample metadata.

```{r}
# Community assignments vs sample metadata
table(ge$aitchison_knn__community, ge$Geographical_location)
table(ge$aitchison_knn__community, ge$Diet)
```

## Exploring and comparing taxon-taxon networks

Since both networks are stored in the same object, we can easily compare them.
For instance, let's check how many edges are shared between the networks,
and whether shared edges have the same sign.

```{r}
# Get edges shared between networks
shared <- intersection(
    rowGraph(ge, "spieceasi"), rowGraph(ge, "sparcc"), keep.all.vertices = FALSE
)

c(
    SPIEC_EASI = ecount(rowGraph(ge, "spieceasi")),
    SparCC = ecount(rowGraph(ge, "sparcc")),
    Shared = ecount(shared)
)

# Same sign in both networks?
table(E(shared)$sign_1 == E(shared)$sign_2)
```

Node degrees in each graph are available in `rowData`, along with taxonomic
information. Thus, we can identify the most connected taxa (hubs) in each
network, and check whether they agree.

```{r}
rowData(ge) |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    select(phylum, genus, spieceasi__degree, sparcc__degree) |>
    arrange(-spieceasi__degree) |>
    head(10)

# Are degrees correlated?
cor.test(
    rowData(ge)$spieceasi__degree, rowData(ge)$sparcc__degree,
    method = "spearman", exact = FALSE
)
```

Finally, let's visualize both networks with nodes colored by phylum. Since
`rowGraph()` adds `rowData` variables as node attributes,
taxonomic information is readily available for plotting.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-dpi: 300

# Define colors for phyla (only those of connected nodes)
connected <- rowData(ge)$spieceasi__degree > 0 | rowData(ge)$sparcc__degree > 0
phyla <- sort(unique(rowData(ge)$phylum[connected]))
phylum_colors <- setNames(palette.colors(length(phyla), "Okabe-Ito"), phyla)
max_degree <- max(rowData(ge)$spieceasi__degree, rowData(ge)$sparcc__degree)

# Plotting function
plot_network <- function(g, title) {
    g <- delete_vertices(g, which(degree(g) == 0))
    ggraph(g, layout = "fr", weights = NA) +
        geom_edge_link(aes(color = sign), alpha = 0.6) +
        geom_node_point(aes(fill = phylum, size = degree), shape = 21) +
        scale_edge_color_manual(
            values = c(positive = "#009E73", negative = "#D55E00")
        ) +
        scale_fill_manual(values = phylum_colors, limits = phyla) +
        scale_size_continuous(range = c(1.5, 6), limits = c(1, max_degree)) +
        theme_graph(base_family = "sans") +
        labs(title = title, fill = "Phylum", size = "Degree", edge_color = "Association")
}

# Plot networks
wrap_plots(
    plot_network(rowGraph(ge, "spieceasi"), "SPIEC-EASI (MB)"),
    plot_network(rowGraph(ge, "sparcc"), "SparCC"),
    nrow = 1
) +
    plot_layout(guides = "collect") +
    plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") &
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 13))
```

Other compositionally-aware methods (e.g., SPRING, CCLasso, or
proportionality-based measures), as well as tools for network comparison,
are available in the __NetCoMi__ package [@peschel2021netcomi]. Regardless of
the method used, the resulting networks can be stored in the same
`GraphExperiment` object, making it easy to compare and integrate them.
